text: How does a secant line become a tangent?
Let us zoom in, and watch the limit take
shape.
Picture a car moving down a road.
Over a whole trip, average speed is straightforward: distance
divided by time.
But a speedometer answers a different question.
How fast is the car moving right now, at
this exact instant?
To find out, zoom in on its position as
time passes.
A secant compares two nearby positions, and its slope
gives the average rate of change.
Shrink the time interval toward zero, and that secant
slope approaches the instantaneous rate, the derivative.
Now let us see the same idea right on
a curve.
Start with f of x equals x squared, a
familiar parabola.
Fix A at the point one, one.
The first coordinate is x; the second is the
function value.
Now place B at three, nine.
Both points lie on the curve.
A straight line through two points of a curve
is a secant.
Its slope is rise over run: change in output
divided by change in input.
From A to B, the rise is nine minus
one, or eight.
The run is three minus one, or two.
Eight divided by two gives slope four.
This is average change across the interval.
Next, B will move closer to A.
Name the horizontal gap h.
Then B has x coordinate one plus h, and
height the quantity one plus h, squared.
The vertical rise is f of one plus h,
minus f of one.
At first, h equals two, so the slope is
four.
Now watch purple B slide along the blue curve
toward A.
The pink secant pivots about yellow A, while the
horizontal bracket shrinks.
At h equals one, the slope is three.
At h equals one half, it is two point
five.
At one tenth, two point one.
At one hundredth, two point zero one.
See the pattern?
Every value approaches two.
The vertical rise shrinks too, but the ratio of
rise to run settles toward a steady value.
For every nonzero h, A and B are still
distinct, and the secant has an ordinary slope.
We never set h to zero in that fraction.
Instead, we ask what the slopes approach as B
gets as close to A as we like.
Their limit is two.
The slopes do not need to equal two yet;
only their limiting value is two.
Here is the algebra that explains the motion.
The secant slope m is f of one plus
h, minus f of one, all divided by h.
Substituting f of x equals x squared gives the
quantity one plus h, squared, minus one, over h.
Expand the square: one plus two h plus h
squared, minus one, over h.
The positive one and the negative one cancel.
That leaves two h plus h squared, all over
h.
Factor h from the numerator to get h times
two plus h, over h.
Since h is not zero, cancel the common h.
Now m equals two plus h.
This cancellation is valid for nonzero h only.
The original fraction at h equals zero would be
zero divided by zero.
Simplify first; then take the limit.
As h approaches zero, two plus h approaches two.
Therefore the derivative f prime of one is two.
Geometrically, two is the secant slopes' limiting value.
Now watch B approach A.
The pink secant pivots smoothly into a green tangent,
the line with the curve's direction at A.
Its slope is two.
On the slope triangle, one unit right is a
run of one; two units up is a rise
of two.
Use point slope form: y minus one equals two
times x minus one.
Distribute, then add one, and we get y equals
two x minus one.
The secant connects two points and measures an average
rate.
The tangent is the limiting line at one point,
and its slope is the instantaneous rate of change.
That is the geometric meaning of the derivative: the
exact rate of change at one point.
We have returned to the car.
On a position time graph, the tangent slope at
an instant is the car's instantaneous velocity.
Keep three ideas: a secant connects two points and
gives average change.
The limit, h toward zero, shrinks their interval toward
an instant.
The derivative is the tangent's exact slope.
For our parabola, f prime of one is two,
and the tangent is y equals two x minus
one.
Thank you for watching.
